newsitem.title: USA: Forecasters say snow, severe cold nears US Plains.
newsitem.headline: Forecasters say snow, severe cold nears US Plains.

text.p: Balmy weather in the U.S. Plains will be replaced by heavy snow in central Texas the next 12 to 36 hours and severe cold is expected for the rest of the Plains by the weekend, meteorologists said.
A winter storm approaching Texas could dump up to 10 inches of snow in the southern Panhandle and snow, ice and rain from Dallas to Little Rock, Ark., forecasters said.

"The heaviest snow could fall in the southern Panhandle area of Lubbock down to Midland where they could be seeing heavy snows of four to six or eight to 10 inches," said Craig Solberg, meteorologist for Freese-Notis Weather.
The majority of the heavy snow will be in the southern fringes of the main cattle feedlot areas, Solberg said.
Amarillo, Texas, Guyman, Okla. and Dodge City, Kan. were only expected to get a couple of inches, Solberg said
Temperatures for all of the main cattle areas were seen diving close to zero this weekend, forecasters said.
There will be below normal temperatures in the U.S. Plains all week, but extreme cold later in the week, according to Weather Services Corporation.

"Right now we're thinking zero to five (degrees Fahrenheit) below in the Panhandle and five to 15 below in western Kansas by Saturday morning," said Mike Palmerino, meteorologist with Weather Services Corporation.
Wind chills will be a factor, especially as cold air moves in on Friday, with wind chill factors of 20 or 30 below zero, Palmerino said.

"It looks similar to that system that came in early December that dropped freezing temperatures right down to northern Mexico," Palmerino said. He said the severe cold could last 24 to 48 hours before it starts to moderate.
Forecasts for cold weather sparked an early rally in U.S. wheat futures, but agronomists said they were not too concerned about damage to the crop.
"I'm not worried about it," said Rollie Sears, a wheat breeder at Kansas State University Research and Extension in Manhattan, Kan.

"The forecasted temperatures are supposed to get down to zero by the end of the week. That's not going to be a really big factor," Sears said. He explained that for the most part, temperatures were cooling down gradually so as not to shock the wheat plants.

"I don't know if the storm will have an impact on the market," said a Texas Panhandle cattle feeder of possible effects the storm might have on cattle weight gains or prices. "It all depends on how much cold and snow we get."
